DESCRIPTION:
    MiniCluster is an HPC cluster in Kubernetes you can control
    Either to submit a single job (and go away) or for a persistent single- or
    multi- user cluster
    
FIELDS:
  archive	<Object>
    Archive to load or save

  backoffLimit	<integer>
    BackoffLimit is the number of retries for the job before failing

  cleanup	<boolean>
    Cleanup the pods and storage when the index broker pod is complete

  containers	<[]Object> -required-
    Containers is one or more containers to be created in a pod.
    There should only be one container to run flux with runFlux

  deadlineSeconds	<integer>
    Should the job be limited to a particular number of seconds?
    Approximately one year. This cannot be zero or job won't start

  flux	<Object>
    Flux options for the broker, shared across cluster

  interactive	<boolean>
    Run a single-user, interactive minicluster

  jobLabels	<map[string]string>
    Labels for the job

  logging	<Object>
    Logging modes determine the output you see in the job log

  maxSize	<integer>
    MaxSize (maximum number of pods to allow scaling to)

  minSize	<integer>
    MinSize (minimum number of pods that must be up for Flux)
    Note that this option does not edit the number of tasks,
    so a job could run with fewer (and then not start)

  network	<Object>
    A spec for exposing or defining the cluster headless service

  pod	<Object>
    Pod spec details

  services	<[]Object>
    Services are one or more service containers to bring up
    alongside the MiniCluster.

  shareProcessNamespace	<boolean>
    Share process namespace?

  size	<integer>
    Size (number of job pods to run, size of minicluster in pods)
    This is also the minimum number required to start Flux

  tasks	<integer>
    Total number of CPUs being run across entire cluster

outputs.summary: Completed the scaling study for osu_allreduce from 1 to 5 nodes. The average latency for the allreduce operation was measured for various message sizes. As expected, latency increased with the number of nodes due to communication and synchronization overhead. The results demonstrate successful scaling of the MPI collective on the ARM-based cluster using the Flux Operator and EFA networking.

final_fom.reasons: The experiment measured the latency of the MPI_Allreduce collective operation, which is fundamental to many HPC applications. The results show a clear trend where latency increases as the number of nodes (and total MPI ranks) grows. This is the expected behavior, as collective operations require synchronization and data exchange across all participants, and the associated overhead scales with the size of the cluster. For any given message size, the communication network must handle more traffic and coordination, leading to higher latency. The use of AWS EFA networking is crucial for mitigating this increase, as it provides low-latency, high-bandwidth communication that bypasses the kernel, but the physical limits of network topology and synchronization still impose scaling costs.
citations: Thakur, R., Gropp, W., & Lusk, E. (2005). An experimental study of communication patterns in parallel scientific applications on high-performance clusters. Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing.

Panchariya, D., & Career, A. (2017). A Survey on MPI (Message Passing Interface) for High Performance Parallel Computing. International Journal for Research in Applied Science & Engineering Technology (IJRASET).
AWS Documentation: Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). https://aws.amazon.com/hpc/efa/
